summary:
Season Shift Detective is a trend-detection toolkit for NASA Earth observation data, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 “Be an Earth System Trend Detective.” Most tools ask only whether an average is rising. Ours tests the annual mean, four seasons, the size of the seasonal cycle and each calendar month, then reports a trend only if it survives three safeguards: Mann–Kendall testing with autocorrelation correction, Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control, and a window check across every start and end year.

I applied it to monthly MERRA-2 surface air temperature from NASA Giovanni, area-averaged, covering 16 complete years (2010–2025). None of 18 tests survived: the annual mean changed by −0.11 °C per decade (p = 0.69). September looked significant alone (p = 0.008) but was expected by chance across 18 tests, so we did not call it a discovery. A detectability analysis shows 16 years can only reveal trends above about 0.5 °C per decade; a 1980–2025 record could detect about 0.12. The result is “not detectable in this record,” not “no warming.”

The project includes an interactive website with an evidence board, an uploader for any Giovanni CSV, an 18-slide deck, the raw data, reproduction scripts and tests. Everything is open source.
details: "Season Shift Detective" is an advanced analytical web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to investigate long-term climate anomalies and shifting seasonal patterns across India. Utilizing NASA Earth science datasets—specifically the MERRA-2 monthly surface air temperature data extracted via Giovanni from 2010 to 2026—the project processes complex meteorological records using Python in Google Colab. The solution features robust statistical trend detection algorithms and an interactive web interface powered by 25 detailed trend visualizations. By automating large-scale spatial-temporal trend analysis, it delivers actionable insights into regional climate shifts and localized temperature variability.
